IDEA: Third-base coach send/hold. Owner: third-base coach and baserunning coordinator. Decision: send or hold a runner on a ball in play to the outfield, several times per game. Cases: every send/hold opportunity league-wide each season, reconstructable from public play-by-play and tracking-derived runner and fielder data. Outcome: runner safe, out, or held, plus the run expectancy that follows. Baseline: hold or send based on outs, score and the coach's read of the arm. Intervention: a pre-game card of break-even send probabilities by outs, base state, fielder arm and runner sprint speed, then a retrospective comparison of actual sends against that threshold.
ASSUMPTION: Public tracking data captures fielder position, arm strength and runner speed well enough to estimate safe probability at the moment the coach decides.
ASSUMPTION: The coach's real-time read adds information that a retrospective model cannot see, which could bias any measured gap toward the tool.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (c) may fail because per-decision run value is small, so the season total depends on how far the club's current sends are from break-even.
UNKNOWN: cubs_current_send_hold_policy
UNKNOWN: public_data_availability_for_ball_retrieval_timing

IDEA: Stolen-base and pickoff-limit exploitation. Owner: first-base coach, manager, baserunning staff. Decision: attempt or decline a steal, especially after the pitcher has used disengagements, many times per series. Cases: every runner-on-first or runner-on-second state league-wide, logged in public play-by-play along with disengagement counts under current rules. Outcome: stolen base, caught stealing, pickoff, and the resulting run expectancy. Baseline: green light for fast runners, conservative for others. Intervention: a per-pitcher, per-catcher break-even model using public pop time, pitcher time to plate, disengagements remaining and runner speed.
ASSUMPTION: Rule changes in recent seasons limit how many seasons are comparable, which reduces (a).
ASSUMPTION: Opponents adapt once a club's aggressiveness becomes visible, so gains may decay. This is a counterparty effect.
UNKNOWN: public_time_to_plate_measurement_reliability
UNKNOWN: cubs_baserunning_green_light_rules

IDEA: Starting pitcher removal timing. Owner: manager and pitching coach. Decision: remove or keep the starter at each batter from the middle innings onward, every game. Cases: every batter faced in the later innings of every start league-wide each season, with pitch count, times through the order and pitch-quality signals from public tracking. Outcome: run value of the next batters versus the replacement reliever's run value. Baseline: pitch-count threshold plus third-time-through heuristics. Intervention: a within-game fatigue and quality signal from velocity, spin and command drift compared with the specific available reliever.
ASSUMPTION: Bullpen workload across the following days is part of the true cost and is hard to price in a retrospective test.
ASSUMPTION: Selection bias exists because starters who stay in were judged to be pitching well, so naive comparisons will mislead without careful causal design.
ASSUMPTION: This overlaps with the explored family of opposing bullpen availability only in data, not in the decision owner.
UNKNOWN: cubs_starter_hook_policy
UNKNOWN: counterfactual_reliever_performance_estimate_method

IDEA: High-leverage reliever assignment. Owner: manager and bullpen coach. Decision: which available reliever enters which inning and leverage state, most games. Cases: every reliever entry league-wide each season, with public leverage index and matchup handedness. Outcome: run value and win-probability change over the reliever's batters. Baseline: fixed roles such as closer in the ninth with a save situation and setup in the eighth. Intervention: assign the best available arm to the highest expected-leverage spot by projected upcoming hitters, subject to rest constraints.
ASSUMPTION: Pitcher comfort with roles affects performance and is not publicly observable, which weakens (d).
ASSUMPTION: Three-batter-minimum rules constrain the decision space and must be encoded correctly.
UNKNOWN: cubs_reliever_role_assignment_rules
UNKNOWN: reliever_rest_and_warmup_cost_public_proxy

IDEA: Pinch-hit and platoon substitution. Owner: manager and bench coach. Decision: pinch-hit, pinch-run or defensive-substitute in a given state, often several times per week. Cases: every late-inning plate appearance league-wide each season where a bench player was available, from public lineups and play-by-play. Outcome: plate-appearance run value and later defensive consequences. Baseline: handedness platoon plus "save the bench for extras." Intervention: an optimizer that prices the bench option value against current leverage and the opponent's likely pitching counter-move.
ASSUMPTION: Counterparty response (the opponent changing pitchers) drives part of the outcome, which partly reintroduces the problem the critique raised.
ASSUMPTION: The value of the bench option in extra innings is small under the automatic-runner rule, but that rule's effect must be verified.
UNKNOWN: cubs_bench_composition_by_game
UNKNOWN: public_availability_of_bench_player_unavailability_reasons

IDEA: Manager replay challenge timing. Owner: manager and replay coordinator. Decision: challenge or not on close plays, multiple times per week. Cases: every challengeable close play league-wide each season, with public overturn records. Outcome: call overturned or confirmed, plus challenge retention. Baseline: challenge when the video room signals high confidence. Intervention: a break-even threshold that weighs overturn probability against the value of the play and the option value of the remaining challenge.
ASSUMPTION: Unchallenged close plays are not cleanly logged publicly, so criterion (a) may fail for the negative class.
ASSUMPTION: This is distinct from ABS ball-strike challenges but may share option-value logic.
UNKNOWN: public_log_of_unchallenged_reviewable_plays
UNKNOWN: cubs_replay_room_confidence_threshold

IDEA: Intentional walk and situational pitching around. Owner: manager. Decision: issue an intentional walk or pitch around a hitter, a few times per week. Cases: every base-out state with first base open league-wide each season, in public play-by-play. Outcome: run expectancy and win-probability change through the end of the inning. Baseline: walk the dangerous hitter with first base open late in close games. Intervention: a matchup-specific win-probability comparison using the projected on-deck hitter and pitcher splits.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (c) likely fails because there are few decisions per club and small per-decision value. The league-wide count may support testing, while the club-level season value stays modest.
UNKNOWN: cubs_intentional_walk_frequency

IDEA: Infield-in and positioning with a runner on third. Owner: manager and infield coach. Decision: play the infield in, halfway or back with a runner on third and fewer than two outs, multiple times per series. Cases: every such state league-wide each season, with public fielder starting positions from tracking. Outcome: run scored or prevented and extra hits allowed. Baseline: infield in late in close games, back otherwise. Intervention: a run-value threshold by batter batted-ball profile, runner speed, inning and score.
ASSUMPTION: Positioning restrictions limit options, so the decision set is narrower than before rule changes.
ASSUMPTION: This may overlap with the explored outfield-positioning family in method but not in decision.
UNKNOWN: public_fielder_positioning_data_granularity

IDEA: Level promotion timing in player development. Owner: farm director and development staff. Decision: promote, hold or demote a minor leaguer between levels, many times per season across a system. Cases: every level change across all affiliated systems each season, visible in public transaction logs. Outcome: next-level performance, injury and later MLB arrival. Baseline: promote after a fixed time or performance threshold at the current level. Intervention: a promotion-readiness model using public batted-ball and plate-discipline data and age-relative-to-level.
ASSUMPTION: This is distinct from MLB call-up translation, but outcomes are confounded because better players get promoted. That needs causal methods such as comparing near-threshold cases.
ASSUMPTION: Minor-league tracking data may be inconsistent in public sources across levels and seasons, which weakens (d).
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (c) may fail because the payoff arrives years later and is hard to attribute to a single season.
UNKNOWN: public_minor_league_tracking_coverage_by_level
UNKNOWN: cubs_promotion_criteria

IDEA: Starter-to-reliever conversion in development. Owner: pitching development staff. Decision: keep a pitching prospect starting or convert to relief, many decisions per year league-wide. Cases: every role switch visible in public minor-league usage logs across systems. Outcome: subsequent velocity, strikeout and walk rates, innings, and MLB contribution. Baseline: convert when command or third-pitch development stalls by a certain age. Intervention: a model using repertoire depth and times-through-the-order decay from public pitch data.
ASSUMPTION: Injury history drives many conversions and is not fully public, which weakens (d).
UNKNOWN: public_role_change_reason_labels

IDEA: Waiver claim decisions. Owner: front office pro scouting. Decision: claim or pass on players placed on outright waivers, many times per season. Cases: every waiver placement league-wide each season is in public transaction records. Outcome: claimed player's subsequent performance and roster tenure. Baseline: claim only if a 40-man spot is open and the player has recent MLB success. Intervention: a ranked claim list from public skills metrics adjusted for 40-man cost.
ASSUMPTION: Waiver priority order and other clubs' claims are counterparty-driven, so outcome attribution fails partly on the critique's concern.
ASSUMPTION: This may be close to the explored roster-rules and minor-league free agent families, and it may share their low ceiling.
UNKNOWN: public_record_of_unclaimed_waiver_players_outcomes

IDEA: Rest-day scheduling for position players and catchers. Owner: manager and performance staff. Decision: rest or start each regular, daily. Cases: every regular's starts and rest days league-wide each season in public box scores. Outcome: subsequent performance, injury list placements, and the replacement's performance. Baseline: fixed rest cadence, day games after night games. Intervention: a fatigue proxy from public sprint speed and bat speed drift triggering targeted rest.
ASSUMPTION: This differs from the explored travel and rest planning family only if the focus is in-game physical decline signals, not schedule structure, so it may be redundant.
ASSUMPTION: Injury causation is not observable, which makes (b) partial.
UNKNOWN: public_bat_speed_sprint_speed_daily_granularity

ASSUMPTION: Across all families, league-wide case counts help (a). Club-specific value (c) still requires knowing how far the club's current practice is from the model's recommendation, which is private information.
ASSUMPTION: Retrospective tests on public data measure league-average policy gaps, not the club's own gap.
ASSUMPTION: In-game decisions such as sends, steals, hooks, relievers and pinch-hits likely satisfy (a) and (b) best. Development decisions such as promotions and role conversions likely fail (b) and (c) on time horizon.
UNKNOWN: cubs_baseline_decision_policies_all_families
UNKNOWN: verified_public_data_sources_for_each_family

text:
IDEA: Third-base coach send/hold. Owner: third-base coach and baserunning coordinator. Decision: send or hold a runner on a ball in play, made several times per game. Historical cases: many league-wide each season in public play-by-play and tracking data, though selection bias exists because only executed outcomes are seen. Observable outcome: runner safe or out at the plate, and the base-out state afterward. Simple baseline: the coach's judgment from runner speed and the fielder's arm. Intervention: a pre-game card plus a postgame audit that scores each send against a run-expectancy breakeven, using public sprint speed, fielder arm strength, fielder distance and the game state.
ASSUMPTION: Public tracking covers enough of the ball-in-play geometry (fielder position, ball location at pickup) to estimate the counterfactual safe probability of held runners, not only sent ones.
ASSUMPTION: The coach can absorb a per-opponent card fast enough for a decision made in about two seconds. If not, (d) holds but the tool has no channel to change the decision.
ASSUMPTION: Value per decision is small, so the season total meets (c) only if the club's current errors are systematic rather than random.
UNKNOWN: cubs_current_send_policy
UNKNOWN: public_availability_of_fielder_pickup_coordinates

IDEA: Starting pitcher removal timing. Owner: manager and pitching coach. Decision: whether to pull the starter before the next batter, made at several decision points in every game. Historical cases: many each season league-wide at the batter level. Observable outcome: run value allowed by the starter's next batter versus the reliever who replaced him, though the counterfactual is unobserved. Simple baseline: pitch-count or times-through-order rule. Intervention: batter-by-batter removal guidance using public in-game velocity and command decay, the platoon matchup and the bullpen state.
ASSUMPTION: In-game velocity and release decay in public data predicts next-batter outcomes beyond pitch count. This is a testable hypothesis, not established.
ASSUMPTION: Failure on (b) is partial. Removal decisions are confounded because managers pull pitchers who look worse, so retrospective tests need careful matching.
ASSUMPTION: Injury-risk and next-start effects of pitcher workload are not observable in public outcome data, which caps the tool's measured value.
UNKNOWN: cubs_pitcher_hook_rule
UNKNOWN: magnitude_of_confounding_in_public_removal_data

IDEA: Reliever selection by leverage and matchup. Owner: manager. Decision: which available reliever enters, and when, made one to four times per game. Historical cases: many reliever appearances each season league-wide. Observable outcome: runs allowed and win-probability change during the appearance. Simple baseline: fixed roles (closer, setup, middle) assigned by inning. Intervention: matching relievers to leverage and to the specific upcoming hitters, using public pitch-type splits and recent workload.
ASSUMPTION: Overlaps the explored "opposing bullpen availability forecast" family only on the opponent side. Own-bullpen deployment is treated here as distinct.
ASSUMPTION: Relievers' preferences for fixed roles and their readiness routines are real constraints that public data cannot capture.
ASSUMPTION: Small-sample batter-versus-pitcher splits are noise. Value would come from pitch-type and handedness models, not head-to-head history.
UNKNOWN: cubs_bullpen_role_policy

IDEA: Stolen-base and pickoff tactics under the pitch-clock and disengagement rules. Owner: first-base coach, baserunners, catcher and pitchers. Decision: attempt a steal or not, and on defense, when to use disengagements. Both occur many times per season. Historical cases: many attempts and disengagements league-wide each season under the current rules. Observable outcome: safe or caught, plus runner advancement. Simple baseline: steal with the fastest runners or when a fixed success-rate threshold is met. Intervention: attempt guidance that accounts for the pitcher's time to plate, the catcher's pop time, the disengagement count and the game state.
ASSUMPTION: Rule changes split the historical sample. Only seasons under the current disengagement rules are comparable, which weakens (a).
ASSUMPTION: Opponents adapt quickly, so any edge may decay within a season.
UNKNOWN: rule_regime_seasons_comparable
UNKNOWN: public_pitcher_time_to_plate_coverage

IDEA: Pinch-hitting, pinch-running and defensive replacements. Owner: manager and bench coach. Decision: which bench player to use and when, made in many games. Historical cases: many substitutions league-wide each season. Observable outcome: plate-appearance result, plus later defensive or baserunning events. Simple baseline: the platoon-advantage rule and a late-inning defensive-replacement habit. Intervention: a substitution plan that values the option of saving bench players, and the player removed, against an immediate platoon gain.
ASSUMPTION: The value of a substitute who is never used is hard to observe after the fact, which weakens (b) for "save the bench" decisions.
ASSUMPTION: For a single club, roster construction limits how many bench options exist, so (c) may be small.
UNKNOWN: cubs_bench_usage_pattern

IDEA: Rest-day allocation for position players. Owner: manager and performance staff. Decision: which regular sits on a given day, made many times per season. Historical cases: many rest days league-wide each season. Observable outcome: the replacement's performance that day and the rested player's performance afterward. Simple baseline: fixed rest cadences, plus sitting players against tough opposing starters or before day games after night games. Intervention: scheduling rest on days when the gap between the regular and the replacement is smallest given the opposing pitcher, park and schedule.
ASSUMPTION: Fatigue and injury effects of rest are mostly unobservable in public data. Only the matchup component is testable, which weakens (b).
ASSUMPTION: Overlaps the explored "travel and rest planning" family. This idea is distinct only if limited to daily matchup-cost minimization.
UNKNOWN: cubs_rest_policy

IDEA: Minor-league level-to-level promotion timing (player development). Owner: farm director. Decision: when to move a prospect up one level, made many times per season across affiliates. Historical cases: many promotions league-wide each season, with public minor-league stats. Observable outcome: the player's performance at the new level and whether he is later demoted back. Simple baseline: promote after a fixed time at the level or after a statistical threshold such as OPS or K-BB rate. Intervention: a promotion-readiness model that adjusts for age relative to the league, park, league environment and the public minor-league tracking data where it exists.
ASSUMPTION: Distinct from the explored "minor league call-up translation" family only if limited to intra-minor-league moves.
ASSUMPTION: Fails partly on (c). Value is long-run and indirect, so it does not add up within one season.
ASSUMPTION: Fails partly on (b). Development outcomes are confounded by instruction quality and the organization's roster needs.
UNKNOWN: public_minor_league_tracking_coverage
UNKNOWN: cubs_promotion_criteria

IDEA: Waiver claims and DFA-pool acquisitions. Owner: front office pro scouting. Decision: claim or pass on players placed on waivers or designated for assignment, made many times per season. Historical cases: many transactions league-wide each season, though claims are limited by waiver priority. Observable outcome: the claimed player's subsequent MLB performance and roster cost. Simple baseline: claim players with recent MLB time and fit for a roster need. Intervention: a ranking based on public pitch-level and batted-ball quality indicators to flag claims undervalued by surface stats.
ASSUMPTION: Fails on (a) for testing claim decisions by one club, because waiver priority and counterparties limit which claims succeed. It passes for league-wide tests of player-quality prediction.
ASSUMPTION: It may resemble the explored "minor-league free agent triage" result, where the model tied a rule based on prior MLB time, so the ceiling could be similarly low.
UNKNOWN: cubs_waiver_priority_history

IDEA: Defensive alignment within current shift rules (infield in or back, corner depth, outfield depth outside the Wrigley wind context). Owner: defensive coordinator. Decision: positioning on each pitch or batter, so many cases per game. Historical cases: very many league-wide in public positioning data. Observable outcome: whether the batted ball becomes an out, and the run value. Simple baseline: standard positioning charts by batter spray tendency. Intervention: positioning that is conditioned on the game state (for example, infield-in breakeven calculations) and on the pitcher's tendencies.
ASSUMPTION: Overlaps the explored "Wrigley wind outfield positioning" family. This idea is distinct only for infield and game-state alignment.
ASSUMPTION: The edges may already be competed away league-wide, which would undermine (d).
UNKNOWN: public_positioning_data_granularity

IDEA: Intentional walks and sacrifice bunts. Owner: manager. Decision: occasional, made multiple times per week. Historical cases: many league-wide each season, though decreasing. Observable outcome: change in run expectancy and win probability. Simple baseline: the manager's convention, or a published run-expectancy table. Intervention: a game-state-specific breakeven calculation that accounts for the batter, the on-deck hitter and the pitcher.
ASSUMPTION: Fails on (c). These decisions are now rare and each has small value, so the season total is likely modest.
UNKNOWN: cubs_current_iBB_bunt_frequency

ASSUMPTION: Across all ideas, (d) is the weakest criterion. Public data is also available to the other 29 clubs, so an edge requires underuse by the Cubs specifically, which is not established.
UNKNOWN: cubs_internal_tools_already_in_use

text:
IDEA: Starter removal timing; owner manager and pitching coach; decision is whether to pull the starter before the next batter, made several times per game in every game; historical cases are every batter faced by a starter in public pitch-by-pitch data, many thousands per season league-wide; observable outcome is run expectancy change over the rest of the inning and the following innings; simple baseline is a pitch-count or times-through-the-order threshold; intervention is a pre-batter estimate combining fatigue signals (velocity and spin drift, release-point drift, recent command), the specific upcoming hitters, and which relievers are available.
ASSUMPTION: Public velocity and release-point drift within a game carries signal about the next few batters beyond what pitch count and times through the order already capture.
ASSUMPTION: The counterfactual is confounded because managers pulled starters when they already saw trouble, so a retrospective test needs matched or instrumented comparisons, not raw outcome comparisons.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (c) may fail because a few runs saved per season could fall within noise for one club, even when league-wide statistical power under (a) is high.
UNKNOWN: cubs_current_starter_hook_rule
UNKNOWN: public_release_point_drift_predictive_value

IDEA: Reliever assignment by leverage and matchup; owner manager and bullpen coach; decision is which reliever enters and when, made in most games; historical cases are every relief entry league-wide in public play-by-play, many thousands per season; observable outcome is win probability added from entry to exit; simple baseline is fixed bullpen roles (closer, setup, middle relief); intervention is a pre-entry ranking that weights upcoming hitter handedness and pitch-type weakness, three-batter-minimum exposure, reliever rest, and preserving high-leverage arms for later innings.
ASSUMPTION: Fixed roles leave value unused, and that value is not already captured by clubs that informally deviate from roles.
ASSUMPTION: Because of the three-batter minimum, the tool has to score a pitcher against the next three or more hitters plus likely pinch hitters, not against a single matchup.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (b) partly fails because reliever availability and soreness are private, so a public retrospective will mislabel some decisions as errors when the pitcher was actually unavailable.
UNKNOWN: reliever_availability_ground_truth

IDEA: Pinch-hit and platoon substitutions; owner manager; decision is whether to pinch-hit or start a platoon partner, made in most games; historical cases are every plate appearance where a bench bat was available, many thousands per season league-wide; observable outcome is plate-appearance run value plus the later defensive and bench-depletion cost; simple baseline is a handedness platoon rule; intervention is an estimate of the platoon split using shrinkage toward population splits, combined with a cost for losing the bench player later and for the defensive downgrade.
ASSUMPTION: Individual platoon splits are noisy enough that a shrinkage model differs meaningfully from both raw splits and a pure handedness rule.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (c) may fail if the per-decision edge is small and the decisions are infrequent for a single roster.
UNKNOWN: cubs_bench_composition_by_season

IDEA: Stolen base attempts and baserunner sends; owner first-base and third-base coaches and the manager; decision is whether to attempt a steal, or send a runner home or to third on a hit, made many times per game; historical cases are every runner-on-base opportunity and every ball in play with a runner advancing, very numerous in public tracking and play-by-play data; observable outcome is safe or out plus the run expectancy change; simple baseline is a runner-speed threshold, or coach judgment proxied by league send rates; intervention is a pre-pitch or in-play probability model using sprint speed, pitcher time to plate, catcher pop time, fielder arm strength, and ball location and exit speed.
ASSUMPTION: The pickoff and disengagement limits and the larger bases changed the break-even steal rate, and some clubs' rules have not fully adjusted.
ASSUMPTION: A send model needs the ball position at the moment of the decision, which public tracking may not expose at enough granularity.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (b) holds well for this family, but third-base send decisions are made in real time with no time for a tool, so the value would come from pre-game coach training and thresholds.
UNKNOWN: public_ball_tracking_granularity_for_send_decisions

IDEA: Infield and outfield positioning within the shift restrictions; owner defensive coordinator; decision is the positioning set per batter and pitcher pairing, made on every batter; historical cases are every ball in play with fielder starting positions, many thousands per season where public positioning data exists; observable outcome is out or hit and the run value of each ball in play; simple baseline is league-default or spray-chart-average positioning; intervention is positioning that conditions on the pitcher's likely pitch mix and location, the count, and the runners.
ASSUMPTION: This family is distinct from the explored Wrigley-wind outfield family because it focuses on infield depth and lateral shading under the shift restrictions, using pitcher and count conditioning.
